we have not found the neutron star associated to either of these SNRs.
we have detected two new SNRs with XMM-Newton and determined their basic physical parameters.
the XMM-Newton observations presented here are consistent with the SNRs being the result of a Type Ia supernova, although the data do not rule out the possibility of a core-collapse event.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have found a new SNR, G85.4 + 0.7, with a shock velocity of ~500 km s−1 and a possible SNR, G085.9 – 0.6.
the SNR G85+0.7, with a radius of ~8.5 pc, is the remnant of a core-collapse supernova, while the SNR G86-0.6, with a radius ~10 pc, is a Type Ia supernova remnant.
the two SNRs are likely to be middle-aged, with the G85.9−0.6 remnant being older than the G85.4 +0.7 remnant.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the X-ray data are consistent with both SNRs being young remnants, with ages of a few thousand years, and that the X-ray emission is likely dominated by the forward shock.
the two SNRs are likely interacting with a molecular cloud, as indicated by their morphology and the detection of a number of discrete sources.
the X-ray emission from both SNRs is consistent with the emission being due to a shock-heated interstellar medium (ISM) rather than a pulsar wind nebula (PWN).
